newsitem.title: UK: Bruton stands firm on IRA truce before talks.
newsitem.headline: Bruton stands firm on IRA truce before talks.

text.p: Irish Prime Minister John Bruton, preparing for elections, vowed on Sunday to retain a ban on ministerial talks with Sinn Fein until its IRA military ally called a ceasefire.
He criticised opposition Fianna Fail leader Bertie Ahern for saying he would meet Sinn Fein, the political wing of the IRA, if he won the June polls that Bruton is expected to call this week.
Bruton told Irish radio the Irish Republican Army should abandon its armed campaign against British rule in Northern Ireland to propel Sinn Fein into all-party peace talks.

"If they wanted to make the decision, which they have got to make eventually, to put aside violence for once and for all, I think they should have made it (by) now," he said. "I won't meet Sinn Fein until there is a ceasefire."
Britain and Ireland put a block on ministerial talks with Sinn Fein in February 1966 after the IRA scrapped a 17-month truce in its guerrilla war.
David Trimble, Northern Ireland's chief pro-British Protestant politician, earlier branded two Sinn Fein leaders who won seats in the British parliament as senior members of the outlawed IRA.

Trimble, leader of the Ulster Unionist Party, said British security forces believed Sinn Fein president Gerry Adams and chief negotiator Martin McGuinness held high places in the guerrilla groups' command structure.
"The security forces in Northern Ireland...regard both Adams and McGuinness as still being members of the IRA's Army Council," he told Sky News.
"They are involved in directing the terrorist campaign, I think there is no doubt about that..," he said.

"IRA and Sinn Fein are inseparable and they are operating as one group, so that Adams and McGuinness must accept responsibility for all the actions of the IRA and of those groups that operate under their influence."
Both men, who will not take their seats in the British parliament in protest against British rule in Northern Ireland, have consistently denied they are IRA members.
They say Sinn Fein, which is a legal party, is committed to a peaceful resolution of divisions between the province's majority Protestants and minority Catholics.
Violence flared again at the weekend when an off-duty policeman was shot dead in a bar in Belfast by members of a small leftist republican militia, the Irish National Liberation Army.
Security sources said guerrillas abandoned a bomb in a car in Belfast on Saturday after the detonator exploded prematurely.

A Protestant man was seriously injured in a savage beating by Catholics in Londonderry and police charged six men with murdering a Catholic who died last Thursday after he was attacked by Protestant mob in Portadown.
